# Is there a rule at all? Bayesian model comparison {#sec-bayes} ::: {.callout-important} ## AI-generated — not for publication The code and prose in this book were written by an AI agent (Claude Code) under human direction. They have not been verified line by line and must not be published or cited as they stand. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Preliminary and unvetted These are exploratory analyses. The models are deliberately minimal, and statements about the published literature come from memory or from an unverified literature pass. Check before relying on any of it. ::: ::: {#setup-bayes .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} %run _setup.py import bayes_rule as B %matplotlib inline ``` ::: ## The proposal Treat productivity as an inference. The learner compares two hypotheses about a class of $N$ items: - **Rule.** There is a default form $R$. Each item is an exception with some probability; an exception's form must be learned separately. - **No default.** Every item's form is an independent draw from the $K$ possible forms. The learner adopts the rule when it has the higher marginal likelihood. The result: this gives the shape of the Tolerance Principle under exactly one choice of prior, a fixed expectation of about one exception per rule. If the learner is allowed to *learn* how exception-prone the rule is, the logarithm disappears. ## Why the evidence is type-based Suppose each item's form is deterministic. After an item's first token, both hypotheses predict its form with certainty, so later tokens carry no information about which hypothesis is right. The evidence is the lexicon of types, $(N, e)$, whatever the token frequencies. Zipfian sampling matters only through which types have been heard so far. This is a principled reason for the principle's most distinctive empirical property, that it counts types and ignores token frequency. It is the same logic as in two-stage models of the lexicon (Goldwater, Griffiths and Johnson), where the generator of forms sees each stored item once. ## Costs Write costs as negative log marginal likelihoods in nats. An unpredicted form costs $\ln K$. **No default:** $\;N \ln K$. **Rule:** each exception pays $\ln K$ for its form, plus the cost of saying which items are the exceptions. Three versions of that second cost: | Version | Prior on the exception rate $\varepsilon$ | Cost of the exception set | |---|---|---| | Sharp | fixed at $\varepsilon = 1/N$ | $e \ln N - (N-e)\ln(1 - 1/N) \approx e \ln N + 1$ | | Sparse | $\varepsilon \sim \text{Beta}(1, N)$: mean $1/N$, but learnable | $-\ln \dfrac{B(1+e,\; 2N-e)}{B(1, N)}$ | | Learned | $\varepsilon \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ | $\ln\binom{N}{e} + \ln(N+1)$ | ### The sharp prior The rule wins when $e(\ln N + \ln K) + 1 < N \ln K$, which gives $$ e \;<\; \frac{N \ln K}{\ln N + \ln K}. $$ {#eq-sharp} Each exception costs $\ln N$ more than a listed item, and each regular item saves $\ln K$. This has the form of the Tolerance Principle, with $\ln N + \ln K$ in place of $\ln N$ and a constant $\ln K$ in the numerator. ### The learned rate By Stirling's approximation $\ln\binom{N}{e} \approx N\,h(x)$, where $x = e/N$ and $h$ is the binary entropy in nats. The rule wins when $$ h(x) \;<\; (1 - x)\ln K , $$ which depends on $x$ alone. The threshold is a **constant proportion** of $N$. The cost per exception has fallen from $\ln N$ to about $\ln(N/e) + 1$, because a learner who knows that 30% of items are exceptions is no longer surprised by each one. ## Results ::: {#tbl-priors .cell tbl-cap='Largest tolerated e against a no-default lister, K = 4, under three priors on the rule\'s exception rate.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} Ns = [9, 16, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 5000] rows = [{"N": N, "N / ln N": round(N / np.log(N), 1), **{r: B.threshold(N, r, B.cost_lister, 4) for r in ("sharp", "sparse", "learned")}} for N in Ns] pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("N") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

The sharp prior declines like 1/ln N; the learned rate is flat; the sparse prior starts like the sharp one and drifts toward a constant.](03-bayes_files/figure-html/fig-priors-output-1.png){#fig-priors} ::: ::: ### The constant is not pinned down The sharp-prior threshold depends on $K$. ::: {#tbl-k .cell tbl-cap='Sharp prior: largest tolerated e for different numbers of possible forms K.' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} Ks = [2, np.e, 4, 8, 20] rows = [{"N": N, "N / ln N": round(N / np.log(N), 1), **{f"K = {k:.1f}": B.threshold(N, "sharp", B.cost_lister, k) for k in Ks}} for N in Ns] pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("N") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

At $N = 9$ the threshold runs from 1 ($K = 2$) to 5 ($K = 20$), so whether 4 exceptions among 9 are tolerated depends on a parameter the argument does not fix. ### The alternative hypothesis matters too The comparison above gives the no-default hypothesis a fixed cost per item. If that hypothesis is also allowed to learn how common the form $R$ is, it becomes the learned-rate model, which is a rule model in all but name. Against it, the sharp rule survives only a handful of exceptions: ::: {#tbl-sharp-vs-learned .cell tbl-cap='Sharp rule against an alternative that learns the frequency of R.' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({"N": Ns, "largest tolerated e": [B.threshold(N, "sharp", B.cost_learned, 4) for N in Ns]}).set_index("N") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: So the Tolerance-like result needs two commitments at once: a rule hypothesis that cannot adjust its exception rate, and an alternative that has no notion of a most common form. ## Summary Bayesian model comparison explains why the evidence should be counted in types. It yields a threshold of the form $N \cdot \text{const}/(\ln N + \text{const})$ only if the rule hypothesis carries a fixed prior of about one exception per class. That prior makes each exception a separate surprise of size $\ln N$. With a prior that can learn the rate, exceptions share their cost and the threshold is a constant proportion. Put differently, the principle amounts to a claim that a rule is a *categorical* hypothesis, one that does not come with a tunable exception rate. That is a substantive commitment, and it is the part that would need independent support.
